catalog_quote: Tone and stress behave essentially in the same way as described by Sasse (forthc.) for the Bireeri dialect. This means in particular: (1) There are only two tonemic units: high and low. High tone is marked by an acute accent (e.g. á), whereas low tone is not marked (e.g. a) unless this could ... (2) The high tone is the marked member of the opposition, low being unmarked. As in the Bireeri dialect, low tones occur more frequently than high tones. (3) Stress is not distinctive; its placement can be predicted from the tonal and/or syllabic structure (see Sasse forthc.). (4) There is a sharp distinction between tonetic and tonemic notation. Plural forms of nouns, for example, have high tone on their last syllable with most speakers. This high tone, however, can be ... [Introduction, on Sasse's Bireeri fieldwork:] ... Heine's attention: (1) Boni, in a similar way as Somali, has a distinctive opposition between lax and tense vowels, this opposition being responsible for an elaborate system of word-internal vowel harmony. (2) Neither stress nor the word-final glottal stop are phonemic. (3) Each noun has a definite and an indefinite form ...

new_statements.quote: A systematic comparative treatment of tone and accent in the Sam languages has not yet been attempted. From our survey, however, it would seem that some tentative generalisations are possible: (1) It is likely that Proto-Sam was a tone language distinguishing between High (á), Low (à) and High-falling tone (â). [...] (3) In addition to three tones (see (1)), Proto-Sam can be assumed to have marked an accent which in most, though not all, cases coincides with High tone. Whether the accent ('a) had distinctive function remains to be investigated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for Aweer word stress is stated anywhere I could open. The best accessible source (a comparative history of the Sam group) treats Boni data as tonal: modern-language forms are transcribed with High, High-falling and Low (unmarked) tones plus a separate accent mark (Table 1, p. 11), and Proto-Sam is reconstructed as a three-tone language with an accent that usually coincides with High tone; Heine says outright that the tonal structure of the daughter languages is not treated (p. 3). Sasse 1979 adds the family-level claim that all described East Cushitic languages are tone languages with a high vs neutral opposition used mainly for grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: Heine notes the accent coincides with High tone 'in most, though not all, cases' and that its distinctive function is uninvestigated; tone distinguishes masculine (High-Low) from feminine (Low-High) in some noun pairs (reconstructed Proto-Sam).
new_statements.domain_note: The quoted statement is about Proto-Sam, not synchronic Aweer; the only Aweer-specific evidence is the transcription convention (tone + accent marks on Boni citation forms, western dialect). Tone-mark glyphs in the quote are garbled in the scanned ('High (a)', 'Low (5.)', '(&)'); rendered here per Table 1's convention (High á, High-falling â, Low unmarked / *à in reconstructions). Not a first-hand statement of Aweer word-stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Aweer = Boni = Aweera (Tucker 1969's name); Glottolog awee1242, ISO bob, no child dialects listed. Heine's data (1977, 1978) are based on the western dialect (around Pandanguo, Lamu District) with central and eastern speakers consulted; Heine 1982 covers several dialects (west, Kijee, Kilii/coastal, Bala/eastern). Not to be confused with the Oromo-speaking 'Galla-speaking Boni' / Waata (Heine's Waata dialect of Oromo, LDAK 4) or the South Cushitic Dahalo (also called Sanye).
